canonical_topic: Transmission, distribution, and the power grid
definition: Transmission is the bulk transfer of power from a power plant to a substation over high-voltage lines; distribution is the transfer of power from a substation to end consumers over much lower-voltage lines. The interconnected set of plants, transmission lines, and substations forms the power grid.
core_idea: Higher voltage is more efficient for moving power long distances but more dangerous, which is why the grid splits into high-voltage transmission and low-voltage distribution segments linked by transformers/substations; the grid's redundant, interconnected structure protects reliability.
key_points: Transformers and substations step voltage up or down between transmission and distribution segments.
The power grid's redundancy — multiple routing paths between any two points — prevents any single line from overloading and helps avoid blackouts from a single point of failure.
Most power lines are overhead, mounted on poles; buried lines are used in some urban areas but are less reliable and harder to maintain, so burying is uncommon in suburban/rural areas.
relationships: Voltage choice for transmission vs. distribution is a trade-off among safety, reliability, and efficiency.
caveats: Buried lines might seem inherently 'better' or safer, but the author notes they are actually less reliable and harder to maintain than overhead lines.
